title: HP Unveils $699 MacBook Neo Rival with OLED Screen and Feature-Packed Design
body:
The personal‑computer market received a fresh jolt this week as Hewlett‑Packard unveiled a new high‑end ultrabook priced at $699, a move that directly challenges Apple’s recently launched MacBook Neo. The device, dubbed the HP Spectre Neo, pairs a 13.5‑inch OLED panel with a suite of premium features—up to 32 GB of LPDDR5 RAM, a 1 TB PCIe SSD, and a full‑size Thunderbolt 4 port—while undercutting the Neo’s starting price by more than $200. By offering flagship‑level specifications at a mid‑range price point, HP hopes to force a recalibration of pricing strategies across the thin‑and‑light segment.

The Spectre Neo’s most eye‑catching component is its 3,000‑nits OLED display, which supports a 100 % DCI‑P3 colour gamut and a 120 Hz refresh rate. Reviewers who have examined pre‑production units say the screen delivers deep blacks and vivid colours comparable to the Neo’s mini‑LED panel, but with lower power draw thanks to HP’s adaptive brightness algorithm. The laptop also incorporates a new “EcoBoost” power management suite that dynamically throttles the Intel Core i7‑14700H processor based on workload, extending battery life to an estimated 14 hours on a single charge—an improvement of roughly two hours over the Neo’s advertised endurance.

Beyond the screen, HP has packed the Spectre Neo with features designed to appeal to both creators and business users. The chassis, forged from recycled aluminum, is only 13.9 mm thick and weighs 2.7 lb, making it one of the lightest OLED‑equipped laptops on the market. A built‑in privacy shutter covers the webcam, while a fingerprint sensor embedded in the power button provides biometric login. The device also supports Wi‑Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.3, positioning it as a future‑proof connectivity hub for hybrid work environments.

Industry analysts view HP’s aggressive pricing as a calculated response to Apple’s disruptive Neo strategy, which saw the tech giant slash its entry‑level model to $799 earlier this year. “Apple forced the entire thin‑and‑light category to rethink value propositions,” says Maya Patel, senior analyst at IDC. “HP’s move shows that OEMs are willing to gamble on slimmer margins to retain market share, especially in regions where price sensitivity remains high.” The gamble could pay off: HP’s Q2 earnings report indicated a 4.2 % decline in ultrabook shipments, a trend that the company hopes to reverse by targeting price‑conscious consumers who still demand premium specifications.

However, the Spectre Neo’s low price tag raises questions about profitability and long‑term sustainability. Critics point out that the $699 price point is contingent on promotional financing and may not reflect the true cost once taxes, accessories, and extended warranties are added. Moreover, the laptop’s reliance on a single Thunderbolt port could limit peripheral connectivity for power users, a shortcoming that Apple addressed by offering an additional HDMI port on the Neo. HP has hinted at a forthcoming “Neo Companion” dock that will add extra ports and charging capabilities, but the accessory’s price has yet to be disclosed.

The launch also underscores a broader shift in the PC industry toward OLED adoption, a technology previously limited to premium devices due to high production costs. As supply chains stabilize and panel yields improve, manufacturers like HP are able to integrate OLED screens without inflating retail prices dramatically. This trend could accelerate the phase‑out of traditional LCD panels in the mid‑range segment within the next 12‑18 months.

Looking ahead, the competition sparked by Apple’s Neo and HP’s counter‑offensive is likely to intensify. Consumers can expect a rapid cadence of feature upgrades, price adjustments, and perhaps new form factors as OEMs vie for dominance in the increasingly crowded thin‑and‑light market. Whether HP’s bold pricing will force Apple to revisit its own strategy—or simply carve out a niche for budget‑conscious power users—remains to be seen. What is clear, however, is that the race for affordable yet premium laptops has entered a new, more aggressive phase, promising both innovation and tighter margins for the industry’s leading players.
